title: Safety-Critical Time-Series Forecasting with spotforecast2-safe
text:
Preface
These lecture notes accompany a course on safety-critical time-series forecasting with the open-source package spotforecast2-safe. They are aimed at students with no prior knowledge of AI regulation and no deep experience with time-series analysis. Anyone who can say at the end of the course why the EU AI Regulation (European Parliament and Council 2024) exists, which four code rules a safety-critical library must obey, and what a complete load-forecasting pipeline built on real ENTSO-E and Open-Meteo data looks like, has reached the learning goal.
crumbs: Preface

title: Safety-Critical Time-Series Forecasting with spotforecast2-safe
text:
A story to start with
Imagine a transmission system operator scheduling a delivery of 65 gigawatts of electric power into the German grid for 08:00 tomorrow. The number 65 comes out of a software system that computed a machine-learning load forecast. The real load at 08:00 is 72 gigawatts. Seven gigawatts short — and in a fraction of a second it is decided whether the lights go out in a major Central-German city.
The story is invented, the risk is not. Software that prepares decisions inside critical infrastructure can have physical consequences from a silent failure that no single human can stop once the dispatch has been issued. It is precisely this concern that drove the European legislator to adopt a regulation on artificial intelligence (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, abbreviated AI Act or EU AI Act) which sets binding requirements for high-risk AI systems: data governance, technical documentation, record-keeping, transparency, human oversight, as well as accuracy and robustness (Art. 9 to 15 AI Act).
The story also explains why this course is not pure statistics: a safety-critical forecasting library can no longer afford silent shortcuts. If data are missing, the system must halt and ask, not simply interpolate. If a training run is repeated, the result must remain bit-identical. If something can be logged, it is logged, because a supervisory authority may need to reconstruct years later who made which decision when.

section: Who is bound by the AI Act?
text:
Who is bound by the AI Act?
The AI Act classifies AI systems by risk (Art. 5 to 7). The pyramid below summarises the four levels: a narrow top of explicitly forbidden applications and a wide base of many systems with minimal risk:








Figure 1: Risk pyramid of the AI Act. The top (forbidden) is very narrow — only a handful of applications are inadmissible under Art. 5. The base (minimal risk) is wide — the vast majority of AI systems fall into the lowest tier and have no obligations. The load forecast covered by this course falls into the second tier (high-risk) under Annex III No. 2 of the AI Act (management and operation of critical infrastructure).





The use case of this course — electric load forecasting for a grid operator — clearly lies in the second tier (high risk), because Annex III No. 2 of the AI Act explicitly lists systems for the management of critical infrastructure. The following chapters show how the obligations from Art. 9 to 15 of the AI Act can be fulfilled technically — not via additional prose documents, but via code that guarantees specific properties.

title: Safety-Critical Time-Series Forecasting with spotforecast2-safe
section: The four code rules (CR-1 to CR-4)
text:
The four code rules (CR-1 to CR-4)
spotforecast2-safe operationalises the regulatory requirements through four non-negotiable code rules. They form the backbone of the entire course; every one of the ten chapters refers to at least one of them.









Rule
Short form
What it is about
AI Act link




CR-1
No dead code
Every function, class, branch is reached by a test or docstring example.
Art. 9, 13


CR-2
Determinism
Same input, bit-identical output. Fixed seeds, fixed iteration order.
Art. 12, 15


CR-3
Fail-safe processing
Invalid inputs (NaN, wrong dtype) raise an explicit exception instead of being silently imputed.
Art. 10, 15


CR-4
Minimal CVE attack surface
A short, versioned deny-list of forbidden dependencies, enforced by a test against the lockfile.
Art. 15



The detailed wording of the rules and their connection to the IEC 62443-4-1 norm can be found in the package’s companion report under Design principles. For this course the rules of thumb suffice:

CR-1 ensures that every line of code that ever runs has also been checked at some point.
CR-2 ensures that you can reproduce a result, even if you repeat it a year later.
CR-3 ensures that the system never silently guesses but always asks back when something is missing.
CR-4 ensures that the list of libraries your system depends on stays small — because each dependency is a potential entry point for security vulnerabilities.

In the ten chapters that follow, you will see how these rules translate into concrete safeguards — at the very moment when spotforecast2-safe does something that another library would just wave through.

Every chapter ends with an Exercises box. The exercises are phrased so that you can paste them directly into the AI assistant Claude (e.g. https://claude.ai or Claude Code in the terminal) to explore the source code of spotforecast2-safe on your own.
A typical exercise looks like this:

Ask Claude: “Show me the source code of spotforecast2_safe.preprocessing.LinearlyInterpolateTS. Explain line by line how the on_missing parameter changes the behaviour. Write a Python example that compares all three permitted values (‘raise’, ‘ffill_bfill’, ‘passthrough’) on the same data snippet.”

We recommend really putting each exercise to Claude rather than googling the answer yourself. The learning effect comes from the dialogue in which you question Claude’s explanation, push back on an insufficient answer, ask for a concrete example, or probe for the connection to the AI Act or to one of the four code rules.

title: 1  Switch on the audit log
text:
1.1 Why log at all?
Imagine that the load-forecasting system from the introduction really did predict 65 instead of 72 gigawatts at 08:00, and the grid is therefore severely under-supplied. The supervisory authority asks: Which data were available to the model at 06:00, with which hyperparameters was it trained, which version of the library was running in production? If the answers are not in a verifiable log, the incident is considered unreconstructable — and the operator has breached their duty under Art. 12 of the AI Act (record-keeping).
spotforecast2-safe therefore writes every action — initialisation of the forecaster, data download, training run, prediction — into a structured log. We switch this log on first, before doing anything else, because the initialisation itself is already a log-worthy action. This practice instantiates both Art. 12 of the AI Act and the discipline of a structured audit log anchored in process rule PR-4. It connects directly to code rule CR-1 (no dead code): every function that is logged has, by definition, been executed, hence is not dead.

title: 2  Loading live data from ENTSO-E
text:
2.1 What the running example in the report was about
The running example in the companion report generates a synthetic load series, because the document must render deterministically and offline. For a course that wants to teach real engineering practice, we replace the synthetic series with real data from the ENTSO-E Transparency Platform — the central database of the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity. ENTSO-E publishes hourly the actual and forecast load for every market zone in Europe.
crumbs: 2  Loading live data from ENTSO-E

title: 2  Loading live data from ENTSO-E
text:
2.2 AI Act link
Data origin is a central concern of the AI Act: Art. 10(2) obliges providers and deployers to maintain data management and data governance procedures which, among other things, document origin, collection method and assumptions about data processing. By pulling the data directly from the ENTSO-E API rather than from a spreadsheet of unknown origin, we keep the provenance explicit and documentable.
Code rule CR-2 (determinism) would be jeopardised by a live API, because the API returns different values tomorrow than today. We solve this by pinning the date window: all students load exactly the same period (DATA_START to DATA_END), therefore receive byte-identical values, and can compare their results with each other.

title: 3  Annotate data gaps instead of inventing them
text:
3.1 Why not simply interpolate?
Linear interpolation (see Chapter 4) fills gaps with invented values. For yesterday’s weather forecast that is uncritical; in a high-risk application under Annex III of the AI Act — such as load forecasting for a transmission system operator — it leads to two structural problems:
The spotforecast2-safe library therefore follows the “annotate, don’t invent” pattern: broken rows are set to NaN, filled in via forward/backward fill only far enough that the lag operator does not crash, and assigned weight 0 in the training loss. The model sees the compromised rows, but they do not pull the gradient.
crumbs: 3  Annotate data gaps instead of inventing them

title: 3  Annotate data gaps instead of inventing them
text:
Auditability disappears. In retrospect an interpolated hour looks to the auditor exactly like a real measurement. But Art. 12 of the AI Act demands that every data-related action remains discoverable in the audit log.
The model learns phantom data. A forecaster that takes the interpolated value as a training target optimises its loss against invented values as well. The expected value of the learned function is biased in favour of the imputer — rather than in favour of reality.

title: 3  Annotate data gaps instead of inventing them
text:
3.5 Step 1 — Mark outliers
mark_outliers runs an IsolationForest on each column and replaces detected anomalies with NaN. The parameter contamination is the expected outlier ratio — keep it small, otherwise the algorithm treats regular load peaks as defects too.

from spotforecast2_safe.preprocessing import mark_outliers

df_marked, labels = mark_outliers(
    df_demo.copy(),
    contamination=0.005,
    random_state=1234,
    verbose=True,
)

n_marked = int(df_marked["load"].isna().sum())
print(f"\nMarked rows: {n_marked} ({n_marked/len(df_marked):.2%})")
print(f"The injected spike at {spike_ts}:  {df_marked.loc[spike_ts, 'load']!r}")

Column 'load': Marked 0.5010% of data points as outliers.

Marked rows: 44 (0.50%)
The injected spike at 2024-01-09 08:00:00+00:00:  np.float64(nan)


The constructed spike was detected — the value is now NaN. The IsolationForest additionally finds about four dozen other inconspicuous-looking hours whose hourly profile deviates from the 2024 pattern; in a production pipeline you would reconcile this suggestion list with domain expertise (dispatcher, grid operator). The list is part of the audit log.

section: 3.6 Step 2 — Fill gaps and weight them
text:
3.6 Step 2 — Fill gaps and weight them
get_missing_weights does two things in a single call:

Imputation: forward-fill, then backward-fill — so that no NaN remains in the series (a technical prerequisite for the forecaster’s lag operator).
Weighting: for every originally compromised row and for the following window_size hours, the weight is set to 0.0. All other rows receive weight 1.0.

The second point is the decisive step: because the recursive forecaster reads a lag window of size window_size at training time, every row inside that window after a gap is also contaminated — it would be trained against the imputed value as a lag feature. Weight 0 excludes it consistently.

from spotforecast2_safe.preprocessing import get_missing_weights

df_filled, weights = get_missing_weights(
    df_marked,
    window_size=72,
    verbose=True,
)

print(f"\nNaN after imputation:                {int(df_filled.isna().sum().sum())}")
print(f"Rows with training weight 0:        {int((weights == 0).sum()):,}")
print(f"Share of excluded rows:             {(weights == 0).mean():.2%}")
print(f"Row identity preserved:             {len(df_filled) == len(df)}")

3.7 Step 3 — WeightFunction as a picklable contract
The forecaster accepts a callable for its weight_func parameter, not an array. Background: the lag matrix is max(lags) rows shorter than the original series; a positional handover would create off-by-N errors. WeightFunction resolves this index-based:

from spotforecast2_safe.preprocessing import WeightFunction

weight_func = WeightFunction(weights)
print(weight_func)

# Call with a timestamp index -> numpy array
sample = df_filled.index[:5]
print(f"\nWeights for {sample[0]} ... {sample[-1]}:")
print(weight_func(sample))

WeightFunction(weights_series with 8783 entries)

Weights for 2024-01-01 00:00:00+00:00 ... 2024-01-01 04:00:00+00:00:
[1. 1. 1. 1. 1.]



3.7.1 Edge case: a window entirely in the danger zone
If every row of a lag window carries weight 0, the weighted loss would collapse to 0/0. WeightFunction detects this and returns None; the forecaster interprets None as “uniform weighting”, so the location remains operational.

zero_idx = weights.index[weights == 0]
window_in_gap = zero_idx[:3]
print("Index in danger zone:", window_in_gap.tolist())
print("Return value:", weight_func(window_in_gap))

WeightFunction: all sample weights for the requested index are zero (the window falls entirely within gap-penalty zones). Returning None so ForecasterRecursive uses uniform weighting.

3.7.2 Picklability (CR-2)
So that the entire forecaster — including the weight function — can later be reloaded deterministically, weight_func must be picklable. An ordinary closure would not be; a WeightFunction instance is:

restored  = weight_func_restored(df_filled.index[:5])
print("Original :", original)
print("Restored :", restored)
print("Identical:", bool(np.array_equal(original, restored)))

title: 4  Handle data gaps explicitly
text:
4.1 Why are data gaps an AI Act topic?
Real sensor data contain gaps. A weather station fails for an hour, an electricity meter is rebooted, a data export drops an empty field. In a pure research notebook this is harmless. In a high-risk application under Annex III of the AI Act — such as the electric load forecast that a transmission system operator uses for dispatch — an unnoticed gap is dangerous. It produces a forecast that is returned with the same apparent confidence as a forecast without a gap; the auditor will never notice afterwards.
Code rule CR-3 (fail-safe processing) therefore requires: invalid inputs explicitly raise an exception instead of being silently imputed. The AI Act underpins this discipline in Art. 10(3) (representativeness, error-freedom, completeness) and Art. 15 (accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity).
pandas, scikit-learn, skforecast, Darts, statsmodels — most tools in the Python ecosystem follow the “silently keep computing” pattern. spotforecast2-safe inverts this default.

title: 4  Handle data gaps explicitly
text:
4.2 The three modes of LinearlyInterpolateTS
Since the major version with the contract switch on_missing, LinearlyInterpolateTS makes the treatment of remaining NaN values explicit. The class interpolates inside the series linearly (limit_area="inside"), so middle gaps are cleanly closed, while endpoint gaps remain and are handled further according to the mode:








Mode
Behaviour
Who uses this?




"raise" (default)
Raises ValueError with a preview of the first gaps as soon as any NaN values remain after interpolation.
Safety-critical pipeline; declares CR-3 actively.


"ffill_bfill"
Fills the remaining endpoint gaps by forward/backward fill.
Migration from legacy notebooks; internally also part of the forecaster’s training contract.


"passthrough"
Passes NaN through unchanged; the next step takes responsibility.
When a downstream imputer (e.g. WeightedAverageImputation) handles the gaps deliberately.

title: 5  Separating training and evaluation range
text:
5.1 Why not split randomly?
In classical supervised learning (e.g. image classification) the dataset is split randomly into training and test ranges. For time series this is a mistake: every value knows its past, and a randomly drawn training set would contain future hours from which the model implicitly learns to predict past hours. The accuracy measurement would be self-deception; it would collapse dramatically in live operation.
We therefore split chronologically: a contiguous initial segment is used for training, a contiguous final segment for evaluation. This split is the simplest variant of a representativeness check demanded by Art. 10(2)(f) and (g) of the AI Act. Code rule CR-2 (determinism) additionally requires the cut point to be fixed as a constant — not random, but reproducible.

text:
6.1 Why does the model need more than the load itself?
The load depends not only on its own immediate history but also on context information: time of day, day of week, holiday, weather. If the model only sees “Wednesday 18:00” and “Wednesday 02:00” as hours 18 and 2, it has no way to recognise that these hours stand in a cyclic relationship to each other and repeat periodically. We encode such cyclic features with radial basis functions (RBF) so that an hour is always similar to its neighbouring hours — including the midnight transition.
Weather is the second pillar. In cold weather the load rises (heating, lighting); on sunny summer days it falls. The model therefore sees per hour a tuple of hourly temperature, cloud cover, precipitation and wind speed. The Open-Meteo API provides these values both retrospectively (archive) and prospectively (forecast) without an API key.

6.2 AI Act link
Art. 10(1) of the AI Act requires that “training, validation and testing data sets […] meet the quality criteria laid down in paragraphs 2 to 4”. One of the quality requirements is representativeness: the model must have seen all relevant seasonal, calendar-related and weather-dependent variations. By training the load jointly with calendar and weather features, we practically deliver the “examination of statistically probable characteristics” demanded by Art. 10(2)(f).
WeatherService enforces code rule CR-3: any gap in the weather data that remains after resampling is reported as ValueError — not silently filled.

title: 7  Instantiate and train the forecaster
text:
7.1 What happens during training?
ForecasterRecursiveLGBM is a wrapper around the gradient-boosting estimator LightGBM. During training the model looks back, for every hour t, at the last lags hours (time steps) and learns a function that predicts the value at hour t from these past values plus the exogenous calendar and weather features. Recursive means: in later prediction the output for hour t is used in turn as input for hour t+1.
lags=168 (= 7 x 24) means: the model sees the last full week as context for every hour — decisive for correctly representing the weekly rhythm (weekday vs. weekend).

title: 7  Instantiate and train the forecaster
text:
7.2 AI Act link
Art. 9 of the AI Act demands a risk-management system over the entire lifecycle; Art. 15 demands an appropriate level of accuracy. Both obligations presuppose that the training run is reproducible: the supervisory authority must be able to reconstruct the model from its documented hyperparameters and seed. This is exactly the scope of CR-2.
CR-4 forbids a short negative list of dependencies in the package (plotly, matplotlib, spotoptim, optuna, torch, tensorflow). The estimator LightGBM is not on this list — deliberately: it is small, actively maintained, implemented in C++ and brings no additional attack surface. A migration to PyTorch or TensorFlow would violate the deny-list.

title: 8  Produce a 24-hour forecast
text:
8.1 Recursive multi-step forecasting
The model was trained to predict one hour at a time, given the last lags=168 hours. For a 24-hour daily forecast the forecaster shifts the 168-hour lag window forward hour by hour:
\[
\hat y_{t+1} = f(y_t, y_{t-1}, \dots, y_{t-167}, \mathbf{x}_{t+1})
\] \[
\hat y_{t+2} = f(\hat y_{t+1}, y_t, \dots, y_{t-166}, \mathbf{x}_{t+2})
\]
At every further step an already predicted value flows into the lag window. This recursion explains why forecast accuracy typically deteriorates with the horizon: model errors from earlier hours propagate to later ones.

title: 9  Measuring accuracy: MAE, MSE, RMSE, MAPE
text:
9.1 Why four measures instead of one?
A load forecast can go wrong in many ways: many small errors in one direction, a single huge outlier, a consistent upward or downward offset. No single measure summarises all of that. We therefore look at four:
crumbs: 9  Measuring accuracy: MAE, MSE, RMSE, MAPE

title: 9  Measuring accuracy: MAE, MSE, RMSE, MAPE
text:
Mean Absolute Error (MAE): the average deviation in load units. Robust, easy to interpret, treats one large and many small errors with equal weight.
Mean Squared Error (MSE): the average squared deviation. Penalises large outliers disproportionately. Has units of “load squared”.
Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE): square root of the MSE; again in load units, but with outlier sensitivity.
Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE): the average deviation in per cent. Allows comparisons between different load levels.
crumbs: 9  Measuring accuracy: MAE, MSE, RMSE, MAPE

title: 9  Measuring accuracy: MAE, MSE, RMSE, MAPE
text:
9.2 AI Act link
Art. 15 of the AI Act (accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity) demands that high-risk AI systems achieve “appropriate levels of accuracy” and declare those in the MODEL_CARD.md. What is “appropriate” depends on the use case. For a daily forecast of the electric load, a MAPE below 4% would be considered state of the art.

title: 10  Rolling-origin backtest
text:
10.1 Why backtest at all?
In the previous chapter we forecast the first 24 hours of the evaluation range and measured three accuracy metrics on it. What if those very 24 hours are unusually good — or unusually bad? A single measurement at a single point on the time axis is not a robust verdict on the model quality.
A rolling-origin backtest shifts the forecast start point step by step through the entire evaluation period and runs a 24-hour forecast at each step. The result is a whole distribution of accuracy measurements: you see not only the mean but also the spread; not only the best- and worst-case but the typical range of variation.
crumbs: 10  Rolling-origin backtest

title: 10  Rolling-origin backtest
text:
10.2 AI Act link
Art. 9 of the AI Act (risk management) demands a testing of the system before it is put into service. Art. 10(3) requires that validation datasets are “representative” — a term that, without an empirical test, remains a mere claim. The backtest provides exactly that empirical test.

title: 10  Rolling-origin backtest
text:
10.3 Code in action

import pandas as pd
import pickle
from pathlib import Path

shared = Path("_cache/shared")
y_clean = pd.read_parquet(shared / "load_de_2024_clean.parquet")["load"]
y_train = pd.read_parquet(shared / "y_train.parquet")["load"]
exog    = pd.read_parquet(shared / "exog.parquet")

# A parquet round-trip drops the `freq` attribute of the DatetimeIndices;
# the forecaster needs it to construct forecast indices.
y_clean.index = pd.DatetimeIndex(y_clean.index, freq="h")
y_train.index = pd.DatetimeIndex(y_train.index, freq="h")
exog.index    = pd.DatetimeIndex(exog.index, freq="h")

with Path("_cache/forecaster.pkl").open("rb") as fh:
    model = pickle.load(fh)


from spotforecast2_safe.backtesting.validation import (
    TimeSeriesFold, backtesting_forecaster
)

# We restrict the backtest to the range for which calendar and weather
# features are available (training + evaluation range from chapter 05).
# That way we avoid asking the forecaster for hours whose `exog` values
# do not exist.
y_bt = y_clean.loc[exog.index.min():exog.index.max()]

cv = TimeSeriesFold(
    steps=24,
    initial_train_size=len(y_train),
    refit=False,
    fixed_train_size=False,
    verbose=False,
)

metrics_df, predictions_df = backtesting_forecaster(
    forecaster=model.forecaster,
    y=y_bt,
    cv=cv,
    metric="mean_absolute_error",
    exog=exog,
    show_progress=False,
    verbose=False,
)
print(f"Number of folds:    {len(metrics_df)}")
print(f"Mean MAE:           {float(metrics_df.iloc[0, 0]):.1f} MW")
print(f"Predictions total:  {len(predictions_df):,} h")
print()
print("First five predictions:")
print(predictions_df.head().round(1).to_string())

text:
10.5 Distribution of errors across folds

import numpy as np

# MAE per fold
mae_per_fold = []
for i in range(len(metrics_df)):
    fold_idx = predictions_df.index[i * 24 : (i + 1) * 24]
    pred_vals = predictions_df.iloc[i * 24 : (i + 1) * 24, 0].values
    actual = y_bt.loc[fold_idx].values
    mae_per_fold.append(np.abs(pred_vals - actual).mean())
mae_per_fold = np.array(mae_per_fold) / 1000   # in GW

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 3.0))
ax.hist(mae_per_fold, bins=12, color="#1F4E79", alpha=0.85, edgecolor="white")
ax.axvline(np.median(mae_per_fold), color="#E07B00", linestyle="--",
           linewidth=1.2, label=f"Median = {np.median(mae_per_fold):.2f} GW")
ax.axvline(mae_per_fold.max(), color="#B33A3A", linewidth=1.2,
           label=f"Maximum = {mae_per_fold.max():.2f} GW")
ax.set_xlabel("MAE per 24-h fold [GW]")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of folds")
ax.legend(loc="upper right", frameon=False)
ax.grid(True, color="#E5E5E5", linewidth=0.5)
for s in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 10.2: Distribution of MAE values across all folds of the backtest, plus the median (dashed) and the maximum value (red line). A narrow distribution means that the model quality is consistent across the evaluation range.

title: 11  Provenance and reproducibility
text:
11.1 What is this about?
Imagine that in two years’ time a supervisory authority asks about a load forecast our system produced on 28 November 2024 at 06:00 for the following day. Can we, today, reproduce that forecast exactly as it was generated back then? If yes, the system is auditable. If not, the authority is entitled to forbid further operation.
Reproducibility presupposes that we have documented all inputs, hyperparameters and intermediate results completely enough for someone running the same code to arrive at the exact same forecast. This chapter is a retrospective: all four code rules and several AI Act articles come together here.

title: 12  Challenge: live load forecasting
text:
12.1 Why a live challenge?
Chapters 02-11 deliberately use a frozen time slice (DATA_START = 2024-01-01, DATA_END = 2024-12-31) so that every student obtains byte-identical results (CR-2). That advantage disappears the moment the model is to run in production: new measurements arrive every hour, forecasters are retrained on a rolling window, gaps appear unpredictably, and the AI Act still demands a verifiable audit trail (Art. 12) and robustness against distribution drift (Art. 15).
The challenge simulates this live setting. You submit a forecast every day; an automatic evaluation workflow compares it the next day with the value finally published by ENTSO-E. The setup is modelled on the well-known scientific competitions:
Methodologically this challenge closely follows GEFCom 2017 (hierarchical load forecasting) and M4 (rolling one-step-ahead setup).

text:
12.5 GitHub onboarding
Technically the challenge runs on GitHub. If you have never worked with it, get yourself up to speed in three steps here: create an account, find your handle, set up authentication. If you already use GitHub actively, you can skip this section and jump straight to Section 12.7.






NoteLearning objective



You have a GitHub account, know your handle, have forked the leaderboard repo and cloned it locally. git push and git pull work without a password prompt.



12.5.1 What is GitHub, what is your handle?
GitHub is a public hosting service for Git repositories (https://github.com/). Every account has a unique username, also called handle or login. The handle is always identical to the final URL component of your profile:
https://github.com/<handle>
Format: 1-39 characters, letters/digits/hyphen, no umlauts. GitHub ignores case when comparing — internally everything is normalised to lowercase.
Why the handle matters here. Submissions go through pull requests. The CI workflow validate-pr.yml in the leaderboard repository reads the author’s login from the GitHub event when a PR arrives and compares it with the github_handles list of the relevant team in teams.yml. Anyone not on that list gets:
ERROR: PR author 'X' not in github_handles for team 'T': [...]
This implements CR-1 (identity & auditability): only you and your team members can submit on behalf of your team.


12.5.2 Create an account

Open https://github.com/signup.
Pick an email, password and username. Important: the username is your future handle and should look professionally solid (tina.musterhuhn looks more serious than xxtina4lifexx).
Click through the email confirmation.
Activate two-factor authentication (Settings -> Password and authentication -> Two-factor authentication). A TOTP app like Aegis or 1Password suffices.



12.5.3 Find your handle (for the registration email)
Two reliable ways:

Click the profile picture top right — the first menu item (“Your profile”) shows your handle.
In any profile URL. Visiting https://github.com/ while logged in redirects to https://github.com/<handle>.







ImportantSend handles to the lecturer



Send all handles of your team in the registration email, otherwise individual members will later be unable to submit PRs. Format like the example below:

Registration team “Lambda Forecasters”
Team-ID: team_lambda
Members and handles:

Alice Mueller — GitHub: alice42
Bob Schmidt — GitHub: bob99
Carol Schulze — GitHub: carol7


Corrections are possible at any time but cost one cycle: you report the fix by email, the lecturer commits the changed teams.yml, and you push a new (or empty) commit on your PR so that CI revalidates.




12.5.4 Set up authentication locally
Otherwise git push asks for a password every time. Choose one of the two variants.
Variant A — SSH key (recommended for daily use).
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your.address@th-koeln.de"
# Copy the public key (~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub) to the clipboard:
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
Then on https://github.com/settings/keys -> New SSH key -> paste contents -> save. Test: ssh -T git@github.com.
Variant B — HTTPS with Personal Access Token.
GitHub -> Settings -> Developer settings -> Personal access tokens -> Fine-grained tokens -> Generate new token. Scope: read/write on the fork of the leaderboard repo. Enter the token as a password on the first git push; Git stores it in the credential helper.


12.5.5 Install the gh CLI (optional but practical)
gh is GitHub’s official command-line tool. It lets you fork, open and merge PRs without touching the browser.
# macOS:
brew install gh
# Windows:
winget install --id GitHub.cli
# Linux (Debian/Ubuntu):
sudo apt install gh
One-off login: gh auth login --web. Then gh auth status is enough to check that everything is in place.


12.5.6 Fork and local clone
Before you can submit, you need a fork of the leaderboard repo — your own copy at https://github.com/<your-handle>/challenge-leaderboard. GitHub rejects direct pushes into the original repo (branch protection), and that is intentional: everything goes through pull requests.
Web UI:

Open https://github.com/bartzbeielstein/challenge-leaderboard.
Click Fork top right -> Owner = your own account -> Create fork.
On the fork page click Code -> copy the SSH (git@github.com:...) or HTTPS (https://github.com/...) URL.
Locally:
git clone git@github.com:<your-handle>/challenge-leaderboard.git

12.7 Submission workflow
Prep done (Section 12.5)? Then now follows the daily routine. It consists of a one-time setup and a recurring submission cycle.

12.7.1 One-time setup — preconditions checklist

Valid GitHub account and handle submitted to the lecturer (Section 12.5).
Fork of the leaderboard repo created and cloned locally (challenge-leaderboard/ on your disk).
uv sync run in the repo root — the Python stack is in place.
ENTSOE_API_KEY is exported in the shell (export ENTSOE_API_KEY=...). Without this key the generator script cannot fetch real data.
The generator script make_submission.py from the course repo is available (see Section 12.8) — or your own.



12.7.2 Submission cycle per target day
In the following, <team_id> denotes your team’s ID (e.g. team_lambda) and <D> the target day in YYYY-MM-DD format (e.g. 2026-05-13).

12.7.2.1 1. Produce the CSV
In the root directory of your local leaderboard fork:
cd .../challenge-leaderboard
python .../lecture/scripts/make_submission.py \
    --team <team_id> --target-date <D>
The script writes the file to submissions/<team_id>/<D>.csv. Inspect briefly: 24 rows, plausible values (DE load typically 40 000 - 70 000 MW).


12.7.2.2 2. Create a feature branch
One separate branch per submission.
CLI:
git switch -c submission/<team_id>/<D>
Web UI: on https://github.com/<your-handle>/challenge-leaderboard open the branch dropdown top left, type the new branch name and confirm with Create branch …. Then locally git fetch && git switch submission/<team_id>/<D>.


12.7.2.3 3. Add the CSV and commit






WarningExactly one file per PR



validate-pr.yml counts the changed files under submissions/** and rejects unless there is exactly one. So add only the one new CSV, no * and no -A.


git add submissions/<team_id>/<D>.csv
git commit -m "submission(<team_id>): forecast for <D>"


12.7.2.4 4. Push the branch
git push -u origin submission/<team_id>/<D>
The success message contains a direct link to create the PR.


12.7.2.5 5. Open a pull request
Web UI: GitHub shows a yellow banner “Compare & pull request” on the repo page right after the push. Click -> fill in title/body -> Create pull request. Important:

Base repository is bartzbeielstein/challenge-leaderboard (the upstream, not your fork).
Base branch is main.
Head repository is your fork, head branch is submission/<team_id>/<D>.

CLI:
gh pr create --base main \
    --title "submission(<team_id>): <D>" \
    --body  "24h load forecast team <team_id>, target day <D>."


12.7.2.6 6. Wait for validation
Web UI: the PR page shows the Checks area at the bottom. After ~15 seconds you see either a green tick or a red cross. On red: go through the steps in Section 12.7.3.
CLI:
gh pr checks <pr-number> --watch


12.7.2.7 7. Merge
When validation is green:
Web UI: button Squash and merge -> Confirm squash and merge -> Delete branch (cleans up the feature branch on the server).
CLI:
gh pr merge <pr-number> --squash --delete-branch


12.7.2.8 8. Sync local main
git switch main
git pull origin main
The feature branch is deleted remotely; locally you can clean it up with git branch -d submission/<team_id>/<D>.






NoteWhat happens after the merge?



The daily scoring workflow runs every day at 07:00 UTC. For every target day before its run it pulls the ENTSO-E ground truth, computes the MAE of every submitted forecast and appends the scores to data/scores.parquet. Then the leaderboard workflow rebuilds the HTML page and deploys it to GitHub Pages. You will therefore see your evaluation on the day after the target day.


Per target day and team: the latest merged valid submission counts. If you submit at 17:00 and want to take a better shot at 22:00, that is allowed — until 23:59 CET on D-1. For the correction add the same path file again (Git sees it as a modification; the validator accepts it).



12.7.3 When the validator is red
The most common error lines from validate_submission.py and how to fix them:







Error message
What to do?




PR author 'X' not in github_handles for team 'T': [...]
Handle missing from teams.yml. Short email to the lecturer. After their commit on main: empty commit on your PR branch (git commit --allow-empty -m "ci: retrigger" && git push), so that the CI recomputes with the new teams.yml.


PR must change or add exactly one submission (found: N)

CSV: expected 24 rows, found N

Target day in path and in file do not match

Negative or NaN values in forecast_mw
Pipeline passed an endpoint NaN through. Check the trim (y.loc[:y.last_valid_index()]) in the generator.

12.8 Baseline implementation
The following script produces a rule-conformant submission. It is a direct application of the pipeline from chapters 02, 04, 06 and 07, with two differences from the main book strand:

Live data window instead of the frozen 2024 slice. We load the last 30 days of ENTSO-E data at training time.
Forecast for tomorrow instead of for a test slice from 2024.


"""
make_submission.py --- produces <repo-root>/submissions/<team>/<D>.csv.

Usage (from the root directory of your challenge-leaderboard fork):
    cd .../challenge-leaderboard
    python .../make_submission.py --team team_lambda --target-date 2026-05-15

Optionally explicit:
    python .../make_submission.py --team ... --target-date ... \
        --repo-root /path/to/challenge-leaderboard

Prerequisites:
- ENTSOE_API_KEY is set in the shell.
- Directory `submissions/` exists under --repo-root.

Minimal pipeline: a pure lag model (168 h ~ weekly persistence)
without calendar/weather exogenous variables. More accurate and
course-near is the full pipeline from chapters 06-08; for the first
submission run this script is sufficient.
"""
import argparse
import os
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

from spotforecast2_safe import ForecasterRecursiveLGBM, LinearlyInterpolateTS
from spotforecast2_safe.data.fetch_data import fetch_data, get_data_home
from spotforecast2_safe.downloader.entsoe import download_new_data


def make_submission(team: str, target_date: str, repo_root: Path) -> Path:
    target = datetime.fromisoformat(target_date).replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)
    train_end = target - timedelta(hours=1)
    train_start = train_end - timedelta(days=30)

    api_key = os.environ["ENTSOE_API_KEY"]
    download_new_data(
        api_key=api_key,
        country_code="DE",
        start=train_start.strftime("%Y%m%d%H%M"),
        end=train_end.strftime("%Y%m%d%H%M"),
        force=True,
    )

    interim = get_data_home() / "interim" / "energy_load.csv"
    df_raw = fetch_data(filename=str(interim))
    df_raw.index = pd.to_datetime(df_raw.index, utc=True)

    load_col = next(c for c in df_raw.columns if "Actual" in c and "Load" in c)
    y = df_raw[load_col].astype(float).rename("load")
    if y.index.inferred_freq != "h":
        y = y.resample("h").mean()
    y = y.loc[train_start:train_end]
    # ENTSO-E publishes "Actual Load" with a few hours' delay.
    # We cut off at the last actually present hour and let the
    # forecaster bridge the gap to the end of the target day.
    y = y.loc[:y.last_valid_index()]

    # CR-3: handle gaps explicitly instead of silently interpolating
    y = LinearlyInterpolateTS(on_missing="raise").fit_transform(y)
    # Forecaster requires a DatetimeIndex with frequency set
    y.index = pd.DatetimeIndex(y.index, freq="h")

    model = ForecasterRecursiveLGBM(
        iteration=0,
        lags=168,
        random_state=2026,  # CR-2: deterministic
    )
    model.fit(y)

    target_hours = pd.date_range(target, periods=24, freq="h", tz="UTC")
    horizon = int((target_hours[-1] - y.index[-1]) / pd.Timedelta(hours=1))
    y_pred_full = model.forecaster.predict(steps=horizon)
    y_pred = y_pred_full.iloc[-24:]

    submission = pd.DataFrame({
        "timestamp_utc": target_hours.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"),
        "forecast_mw": y_pred.values.round(2),
    })

    submissions_dir = repo_root / "submissions"
    if not submissions_dir.is_dir():
        raise SystemExit(
            f"Directory '{submissions_dir}' not found. "
            f"Call from the root directory of the challenge-leaderboard repo "
            f"is expected, or specify --repo-root explicitly."
        )

    out = submissions_dir / team / f"{target_date}.csv"
    out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    submission.to_csv(out, index=False)
    return out


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--team", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--target-date", required=True,
                        help="YYYY-MM-DD (UTC date of forecast target)")
    parser.add_argument("--repo-root", type=Path, default=Path.cwd(),
                        help="root directory of the challenge-leaderboard "
                             "repo (default: current working directory)")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    path = make_submission(args.team, args.target_date, args.repo_root.resolve())
    print(f"Submission written: {path}")

12.9 Scoring methodology in detail
For every valid submission of team t for target day D the scoring script computes:
\[
\text{MAE}_{t,D} \;=\; \frac{1}{24} \sum_{h=0}^{23}
\bigl|\, y^{(\text{forecast})}_{t,D,h} - y^{(\text{actual})}_{D,h} \,\bigr|
\]
with \(y^{(\text{actual})}_{D,h}\) being the ENTSO-E final value for hour h. Additionally, RMSE and MAPE are logged (for diagnostics, not for the ranking).
The public ranking is the rolling 7-day mean:
\[
\overline{\text{MAE}}_t(D_{\text{today}}) \;=\;
\frac{1}{7} \sum_{k=0}^{6} \text{MAE}_{t,\,D_{\text{today}} - k}
\]
(omitting days without a valid submission). Anyone who fails to reach four valid submissions in a given week does not appear in the main ranking that week but in a “quota” side ranking. The interim presentation on 2026-06-22 requires at least 30 valid submissions.

12.10 Evaluation architecture (GitHub Actions + Pages)
                 +---------------------------+
   Team forks  ->|  challenge-leaderboard    |
   and opens PR |  (public GitHub repo)     |
                 +-------------+-------------+
                               |
              on: pull_request |
                               v
                 +---------------------------+
                 |  validate-pr.yml          | -- schema check
                 |                           |    deadline check
                 |                           |    team-auth check
                 +-------------+-------------+
                               | green -> auto-merge
                               v
                 +---------------------------+
   cron 0 7 * * *|  score-daily.yml          | -- ENTSO-E final-load pull
                 |                           |    MAE per team
                 |                           |    append data/scores.parquet
                 +-------------+-------------+
                               | workflow_run
                               v
                 +---------------------------+
                 |  build-and-deploy.yml     | -- aggregate, HTML render
                 |                           |    deploy to gh-pages
                 +-------------+-------------+
                               |
                               v
                 Leaderboard on GitHub Pages,
                 public, readable without login.
Three properties are constitutive here:

Auditability (Art. 12 AI Act): every submission, every scoring result and every leaderboard state is a commit in the Git history; nothing is overwritten.
Determinism (CR-2): the scoring workflow pins its dependencies in uv.lock, sets PYTHONHASHSEED=0 and freezes the ENTSO-E response as a snapshot in the same commit that writes the score result.
Fail-safe (CR-3): if a single value is missing in the ENTSO-E pull, the validator (with LinearlyInterpolateTS(on_missing="raise")) aborts and does not publish a partial result; scoring is postponed by one day.

Complete workflow snippets live in the challenge-leaderboard repo (path: .github/workflows/).

13.5 Live example — generate ŷ₀ end-to-end
The cells below are the live pipeline: every render of this chapter downloads today’s ENTSO-E actuals, trains a fresh Optuna-tuned LightGBM forecaster on the available data, and writes a validated CSV into your forked leaderboard’s submission slot for tomorrow. Optuna drives a Bayesian (TPE) search over the LightGBM hyperparameters; the other three approaches (Lazy, Defaults, SpotOptim) are introduced for comparison in chapters 07 through 10.

import logging, os
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.WARNING)

# Isolate this chapter's storage from chapter 14 -----------------------------
# download_new_data() writes the merged ENTSO-E mirror to
# <SPOTFORECAST2_DATA>/interim/energy_load.csv, and MultiTask persists tuned
# models, tuning results, and logs under <SPOTFORECAST2_CACHE>. Both default to
# a single shared location in $HOME, so chapters 13 and 14 would otherwise read
# and write the *same* interim download. Pinning per-chapter homes here — before
# any download or MultiTask call — gives this chapter its own download, cache,
# and log directory. The package reads both env vars at call time via
# get_data_home() / get_cache_home(), so setting them now is sufficient.
os.environ["SPOTFORECAST2_DATA"]  = str(Path.home() / "spotforecast2_data"  / "ddmo_ch13_live")
os.environ["SPOTFORECAST2_CACHE"] = str(Path.home() / ".spotforecast2_cache" / "ddmo_ch13_live")

from spotforecast2_safe.data import Period
from spotforecast2_safe.downloader.entsoe import download_new_data
from spotforecast2_safe.data.fetch_data import get_data_home
from spotforecast2_safe.configurator.config_entsoe import ConfigEntsoe
from spotforecast2.tasks.task_entsoe import (
    entsoe_data_loader,
    entsoe_test_data_loader,
    entsoe_lgbm_factory,
)
from spotforecast2.multitask import MultiTask


13.5.1 Dynamic date constants
Every date is derived from pd.Timestamp.now(tz="UTC").normalize() so the chapter stays correct on every render. The convention follows the canonical bart26b/CLAUDE.md Date-range rule:

y_{-1} = yesterday’s 24 hourly DE Actual Load values (UTC day D-1)
ŷ_{-1} = the model’s prediction for the same window (used by chapters 08–10 as the scorable exemplar)
y_0 = today’s 24 h (UTC day D); the real live target — not scorable until ~D+1 06:00 UTC when ENTSO-E publishes final actuals


NOW_UTC = pd.Timestamp.now(tz="UTC")
TODAY_UTC = NOW_UTC.normalize()
YESTERDAY_UTC = TODAY_UTC - pd.Timedelta(days=1)
TOMORROW_UTC = TODAY_UTC + pd.Timedelta(days=1)

START_DOWNLOAD = "202201010000"

print(f"NOW_UTC       = {NOW_UTC}")

print(f"TOMORROW_UTC  = {TOMORROW_UTC}  (target day = y_0)")

13.5.2 Download today’s ENTSO-E actuals
download_new_data is incremental: subsequent calls only fetch ranges not already on disk. After the call, we verify coverage and abort loudly if the merged interim CSV does not extend through D-1 23:00 UTC — a stale download would silently shorten the prediction window.

api_key = os.environ.get("ENTSOE_API_KEY")
assert api_key, "ENTSOE_API_KEY must be set in the environment (see Step 3 above)."

download_new_data(
    api_key=api_key,
    country_code="DE",
    start=START_DOWNLOAD,
    end=END_DOWNLOAD,
    force=False,
)

interim_csv = get_data_home() / "interim" / "energy_load.csv"

interim.index = pd.to_datetime(interim.index, utc=True)

if interim.index.max() < required_last:
    raise RuntimeError(

13.5.3 Determine the live training cutoff and forecast horizon
At submission time the ENTSO-E intra-day actuals usually cover only part of today, so we cannot anchor end_train_default at today 23:00 UTC. Instead we anchor at the latest hour for which Actual Load is non-NaN, floor it to a clean hour boundary, and compute how many hourly forecast steps we need to reach the end of tomorrow. After training we slice tomorrow’s 24 hourly steps out of the longer forecast — those are the y_0 rows we submit.

LAST_TARGET = TOMORROW_UTC + pd.Timedelta(hours=23)
LAST_FULL_HOUR = interim["Actual Load"].dropna().index.max().floor("h")

NoteWhy is predict_size usually larger than 24?



predict_size is not “how many hours we want to submit.” It is the number of hourly steps the recursive forecaster must produce, starting at the first hour after the last known actual, until it reaches the end of tomorrow. The 24 rows we submit are then sliced out of that longer forecast.
The math, step by step:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\texttt{FIRST\_PRED}  &= \texttt{LAST\_FULL\_HOUR} + 1\,\text{h} \\
\texttt{LAST\_TARGET} &= \texttt{TOMORROW\_UTC} + 23\,\text{h} \\
\texttt{LIVE\_N\_STEPS} &= \frac{\texttt{LAST\_TARGET} - \texttt{FIRST\_PRED}}{1\,\text{h}} + 1
\end{aligned}
\]
The + 1 is because both endpoints are inclusive (we need the hour FIRST_PRED and the hour LAST_TARGET).
Decomposing the horizon into two segments makes it obvious where the extra steps come from:
\[
\underbrace{\texttt{LIVE\_N\_STEPS}}_{\text{total recursion}}
= \underbrace{(24 - \texttt{LAST\_FULL\_HOUR.hour} - 1)}_{\text{bridge: rest of today}}
+ \underbrace{24}_{y_0:\text{ tomorrow}}
\]
A worked example. Suppose the chapter is rendered at 18:30 UTC and ENTSO-E’s intra-day feed currently publishes Actual Load through 17:00 UTC today. Then:

LAST_FULL_HOUR = today 17:00 UTC
FIRST_PRED = today 18:00 UTC
LAST_TARGET = tomorrow 23:00 UTC
bridge hours = 24 - 17 - 1 = 6 (today 18:00, 19:00, 20:00, 21:00, 22:00, 23:00)
target hours = 24 (tomorrow 00:00 … 23:00)
LIVE_N_STEPS = 6 + 24 = 30

Why can’t we just ask the model for 24 steps and start at tomorrow 00:00? Because the LightGBM forecaster behind entsoe_lgbm_factory is recursive: its feature row for hour \(h+1\) uses the lag-1 value \(\hat{y}_h\) that it produced one step earlier (together with lag-2, lag-24, calendar, and weather features). It cannot “jump” over the 6 bridge hours; each prediction is built from the chain of preceding predictions. The bridge hours are scaffolding the recursion needs to reach tomorrow — once it has, the next cell slices them off:
y0 = future.loc[TOMORROW_UTC:LAST_TARGET]   # exactly 24 rows

13.5.4 Build the live ConfigEntsoe
All inputs to the pipeline travel on a single configuration object. The hooks (data_loader, test_data_loader, forecaster_factory) are the same ones the bart26b publication uses. The training-window parameters and tuning budgets follow the canonical defaults. The ConfigEntsoe documentation is at https://sequential-parameter-optimization.github.io/spotforecast2-safe/docs/reference/configurator.config_entsoe.ConfigEntsoe.html
We pass cv_block_size=PREDICT_SIZE (= 24) so the rolling cross-validation scores a fixed 24-hour-ahead block, decoupled from the render-dependent live horizon predict_size=LIVE_N_STEPS. Chapter 14 derives why this matters at Section 14.6.2.

TRAIN_SIZE = pd.Timedelta(days=365 * 3)
PREDICT_SIZE = 24
REFIT_SIZE = 7
NUMBER_FOLDS = 10
DELTA_VAL = pd.Timedelta(hours=PREDICT_SIZE * REFIT_SIZE * NUMBER_FOLDS)

live_config = ConfigEntsoe(
    country_code="DE",
    data_filename="interim/energy_load.csv",
    targets=["Actual Load"],
    agg_weights=[1.0],
    bounds=[(-1e9, 1e9)],
    data_loader=entsoe_data_loader,
    test_data_loader=entsoe_test_data_loader,
    forecaster_factory=entsoe_lgbm_factory,
    periods=[Period(name='daily', n_periods=12, column='hour', input_range=(1, 24))],
    lags_consider=[1, 2, 24],
    train_size=TRAIN_SIZE,
    end_train_default=LAST_FULL_HOUR.isoformat(),
    delta_val=DELTA_VAL,
    predict_size=LIVE_N_STEPS,
    cv_block_size=PREDICT_SIZE,
    refit_size=REFIT_SIZE,
    n_trials_optuna=30,
    n_trials_spotoptim=7,
    n_initial_spotoptim=5,
    random_state=42,
    on_weather_failure="skip",
)
live_config.data_frame_name = "ddmo-live"
print("live_config ready:", live_config.data_frame_name,
      "predict_size=", live_config.predict_size,
      "end_train_default=", live_config.end_train_default)

The MultiTask orchestrator runs the full pipeline: prepare data, detect outliers, impute, build exogenous (calendar / day-night / weather / holiday) features, tune hyperparameters with Optuna, fit the final forecaster, and return a prediction package. 14.1 Overview
Chapter 13 is a generic template: any team can render it, substitute a placeholder, and submit. This chapter is team_4’s tuned variant. Every safety contract from chapter 13 carries over (deadline check, 24-row schema, strictly-positive forecasts, fail-loud ENTSO-E coverage assertion); only the modelling configuration changes.
What this chapter changes relative to Chapter 13:

title: 14  Team 4 live submission — advanced setup
text:
All five seasonal Periods instead of daily alone — weekly, monthly, quarterly, and yearly RBF encodings join the daily one.
Candidate lags chosen dynamically from the data — the PACF-significant lags (1) rather than the baseline’s hard-coded [1, 2, 24].
include_weather_windows=True, include_holiday_features=True, poly_features_degree=2 — temperature, DE/NW public holidays, and bilinear calendar-by-weather interactions enter the exogenous matrix. The interactions are capped at max_poly_features=10, keeping only the ten most informative ones (by mutual information).
SpotOptim budget kept small for a fast live render — 6 / 5 (trials / initial evaluations) with number_folds=10. This is the one knob still dialled down; raising it deepens the search at the cost of render time.

14.5 Live pipeline
The cells below are the live team_4 pipeline. Every render downloads today’s ENTSO-E actuals, tunes an LGBM forecaster with the advanced configuration, and writes a validated CSV for tomorrow.

import logging, os
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.WARNING)

# Isolate this chapter's storage from chapter 13 -----------------------------
# download_new_data() writes the merged ENTSO-E mirror to
# <SPOTFORECAST2_DATA>/interim/energy_load.csv, and MultiTask persists tuned
# models, tuning results, and logs under <SPOTFORECAST2_CACHE>. Both default to
# a single shared location in $HOME, so chapters 13 and 14 would otherwise read
# and write the *same* interim download. Pinning per-chapter homes here — before
# any download or MultiTask call — gives this chapter its own download, cache,
# and log directory. The package reads both env vars at call time via
# get_data_home() / get_cache_home(), so setting them now is sufficient.
os.environ["SPOTFORECAST2_DATA"]  = str(Path.home() / "spotforecast2_data"  / "ddmo_ch14_team4")
os.environ["SPOTFORECAST2_CACHE"] = str(Path.home() / ".spotforecast2_cache" / "ddmo_ch14_team4")

from spotforecast2_safe.data import Period
from spotforecast2_safe.downloader.entsoe import download_new_data
from spotforecast2_safe.data.fetch_data import get_data_home
from spotforecast2_safe.configurator.config_entsoe import ConfigEntsoe
from spotforecast2.tasks.task_entsoe import (
    entsoe_data_loader,
    entsoe_test_data_loader,
    entsoe_lgbm_factory,
)
from spotforecast2.multitask import MultiTask


14.5.1 Dynamic date constants
Every date is derived from pd.Timestamp.now(tz="UTC").normalize() so the chapter stays correct on every render — same convention as Section 13.5.

NOW_UTC = pd.Timestamp.now(tz="UTC")
TODAY_UTC = NOW_UTC.normalize()
YESTERDAY_UTC = TODAY_UTC - pd.Timedelta(days=1)
TOMORROW_UTC = TODAY_UTC + pd.Timedelta(days=1)

START_DOWNLOAD = "202201010000"
# Fetch through *tomorrow* so the interim file lands two things: (a) the most
# current ENTSO-E actuals already published today --- which shrinks the
# recursive bridge and horizon --- and (b) ENTSO-E's own day-ahead
# `Forecasted Load` for the target day, used only for the comparison plot in
# @sec-team4-vs-entsoe (the model never sees it). Future timestamps simply
# carry no Actual Load yet, so the training cutoff and horizon are unchanged.
END_DOWNLOAD = (TOMORROW_UTC + pd.Timedelta(days=1)).strftime("%Y%m%d%H%M")

print(f"NOW_UTC       = {NOW_UTC}")
print(f"TODAY_UTC     = {TODAY_UTC}")
print(f"TOMORROW_UTC  = {TOMORROW_UTC}  (target day = y_0)")
print(f"END_DOWNLOAD  = {END_DOWNLOAD}  (covers tomorrow for ENTSO-E's day-ahead forecast)")

NOW_UTC       = 2026-05-31 19:24:33.068407+00:00
TODAY_UTC     = 2026-05-31 00:00:00+00:00
TOMORROW_UTC  = 2026-06-01 00:00:00+00:00  (target day = y_0)
END_DOWNLOAD  = 202606020000  (covers tomorrow for ENTSO-E's day-ahead forecast)




14.5.2 Download today’s ENTSO-E actuals and ENTSO-E’s own day-ahead Forecasted Load

api_key = os.environ.get("ENTSOE_API_KEY")
assert api_key, "ENTSOE_API_KEY must be set in the environment."

download_new_data(
    api_key=api_key,
    country_code="DE",
    start=START_DOWNLOAD,
    end=END_DOWNLOAD,
    force=True,
    keep_forecast_future=True,
)

keep_forecast_future=True is the one argument that differs from the training chapters’ download. By default download_new_data drops every row after now when it builds the interim file — the leakage-free input a model must train on. That default would also erase ENTSO-E’s day-ahead Forecasted Load for the target day, leaving the baseline comparison in Section 14.6.11 with nothing to plot. The flag keeps those future rows, so tomorrow’s published forecast survives; the future Actual Load is still blank, so no future target leaks into training (the leakage guard in Section 14.6.9 re-checks this).


14.5.3 The interim energy-load frame
download_new_data merges every ENTSO-E pull into one tidy file, interim/energy_load.csv, under the package data home (get_data_home()). That file is the single source the rest of the chapter reads from. Its shape is worth knowing before the cells below slice it:

Index — Time (UTC) parsed to a timezone-aware DatetimeIndex, stepping in 15-minute (quarter-hour) increments. It runs from START_DOWNLOAD (2022-01-01 00:00 UTC) through END_DOWNLOAD (the day after tomorrow), so the frame deliberately extends past now into the target day.
Actual Load — ENTSO-E’s German Actual Total Load in MW, the forecaster’s target. It is populated only up to the last quarter-hour ENTSO-E has actually published; every timestamp after that — including all of the target day — is blank (NaN). The last non-blank stamp is what Section 14.5.6 turns into end_train.
Forecasted Load — ENTSO-E’s own day-ahead load forecast in MW, published around midday D-1. Because it is a forecast, it covers the future hours Actual Load does not, which is exactly why END_DOWNLOAD reaches into tomorrow. The model never trains on this column (the leakage guard in Section 14.6.9 enforces that); it serves only as the independent baseline in Section 14.6.11 and the overlay in Figure 14.2.
Actual — a legacy ENTSO-E column carried through the download verbatim; it is empty for DE load and the pipeline ignores it.

The cell below loads the file, coerces the index to UTC, and runs two fail-loud coverage checks. The first guards the frame’s index: it must reach at least D-1 23:00 UTC so the exogenous features and the forecast bridge have somewhere to land. That index is kept fresh by Forecasted Load (which extends into the future), so it does not speak to the target’s freshness. The second check therefore guards the target directly. It cannot demand the actuals reach D-1 23:00, because ENTSO-E publishes the German actual load with a normal lag of a few hours — early in the UTC day the actuals legitimately trail that bar. Instead it allows the last published Actual Load stamp to lag now by up to MAX_ACTUAL_LAG (24 h here, easily raised), failing only when the feed is genuinely stale — the index looking current while the training history quietly ended a day or more early.

interim_csv = get_data_home() / "interim" / "energy_load.csv"
interim = pd.read_csv(interim_csv, index_col=0, parse_dates=True)
interim.index = pd.to_datetime(interim.index, utc=True)

required_last = TODAY_UTC - pd.Timedelta(hours=1)
if interim.index.max() < required_last:
    raise RuntimeError(
        f"ENTSO-E coverage is stale: last interim row is {interim.index.max()} "
        f"but the chapter requires at least {required_last}. "
        "Re-run download_new_data(..., force=True) or check the ENTSO-E API."
    )

# ENTSO-E publishes the German actual load with a normal lag of a few hours,
# so the actuals legitimately trail `now` (especially early in the UTC day).
# Guard only against a genuinely stale feed: the last published actual must lie
# within MAX_ACTUAL_LAG of now. Raise the tolerance if your feed lags more.
MAX_ACTUAL_LAG = pd.Timedelta(hours=36)
last_actual = interim["Actual Load"].dropna().index.max()
if last_actual < NOW_UTC - MAX_ACTUAL_LAG:
    lag_h = int((NOW_UTC - last_actual) / pd.Timedelta(hours=1))
    raise RuntimeError(
        f"Actual Load is stale: last published actual is {last_actual}, "
        f"{lag_h} h before now ({NOW_UTC}); tolerance is "
        f"{int(MAX_ACTUAL_LAG / pd.Timedelta(hours=1))} h. "
        "Re-run download_new_data(..., force=True) or wait for ENTSO-E to "
        "publish more recent actuals."
    )
print(f"interim CSV last row: {interim.index.max()}")
print(interim["Actual Load"].dropna().tail(6))

14.5.4 Extract ENTSO-E’s day-ahead Forecasted Load
ENTSO-E’s own day-ahead forecast is used twice downstream — as the overlay in Figure 14.1 and as the scored baseline in Section 14.6.11 — so we pull it out of the interim frame once, here, and keep it as a standalone Series. It is resampled onto the hourly grid (the mean of each hour’s four quarter-hour values, matching how prepare_data() aggregates the actuals in Section 14.6.3), so it lines up directly with the forecaster’s hourly output for error computations. The trailing .dropna() keeps only the hours ENTSO-E has actually published a forecast for. The model never trains on these values — the leakage guard in Section 14.6.9 enforces that; predictions_entsoe is an independent baseline only.

predictions_entsoe = interim["Forecasted Load"].resample("h").mean().dropna()
predictions_entsoe.name = "Forecasted Load"

      f"| {predictions_entsoe.index.min()} → {predictions_entsoe.index.max()}")

14.5.5 Native resolution: 15-minute actuals aggregated to hourly
ENTSO-E publishes the German Actual Total Load at 15-minute (quarter-hour) resolution, and download_new_data stores it verbatim — the interim/energy_load.csv index steps in 15-minute increments, not hourly. The hourly grid the forecaster trains on is produced later, inside prepare_data() (Section 14.6.3): it calls agg_and_resample_data(rule="h", by="mean") (in spotforecast2_safe.preprocessing.curate_data), which replaces the four quarter-hour values in each hour with their mean. The mean — not the sum — is the correct aggregation because load is an average power level over the interval, not an accumulated quantity. The cell below confirms the native cadence of the freshly downloaded interim frame.

14.5.6 Training cutoff and forecast horizon
Identical mechanics to Section 13.5: anchor end_train at the last full hour of Actual Load, then forecast forward through tomorrow 23:00 UTC and slice the 24 rows we submit.

LAST_TARGET = TOMORROW_UTC + pd.Timedelta(hours=23)
LAST_FULL_HOUR = interim["Actual Load"].dropna().index.max().floor("h")
FIRST_PRED = LAST_FULL_HOUR + pd.Timedelta(hours=1)
LIVE_N_STEPS = int((LAST_TARGET - FIRST_PRED).total_seconds() // 3600) + 1

print(f"end_train (inclusive): {LAST_FULL_HOUR}")
print(f"first forecast step  : {FIRST_PRED}")
print(f"last forecast step   : {LAST_TARGET}")

14.5.7 Data availability vs. the requested interval
It is tempting to assume that at render time now, the Actual Load series reaches now - 1 h — the last completed hour. ENTSO-E does not work that way: the German actual total load is published with a lag, so the last observed hour y_e can sit well before now - 1 h. The span between them is publication lag, not missing data, and y_e is exactly the end_train cutoff fixed in Section 14.5.6.
This matters because of how the frame is built. download_new_data extends the merged index into the future via Forecasted Load, so interim runs to roughly now, while Actual Load stops at y_e. When prepare_data() (Section 14.6.3) resamples to an hourly grid it spans that full index, so the hours after y_e carry no target and show up as NaN. They are not gaps in the historical record — they are the recent tail ENTSO-E has not published yet, the very interval the forecast bridge is built to span. The curation and imputation steps (Section 14.6.4, Section 14.6.5) will encounter them, but they are harmless: end_train slices them out of the training target y_train, so the model never fits them.
The table below makes these boundaries explicit so the trailing NaN count seen later is not mistaken for corrupt history. (The symbol y_e here marks a data-availability boundary — the last observed actual hour — and is distinct from the forecast notation y_0 / y_{-1}, which name the target day and the day before it.)

14.5.8 Visualization of the training data and ENTSO-E’s own day-ahead Forecasted Load
Figure 14.1 shows the full training series the forecaster is tuned on. It is assembled in a single line, train_view = interim.loc[:LAST_FULL_HOUR, ["Actual Load"]].dropna(), which is worth unpacking. The .loc[:LAST_FULL_HOUR, ["Actual Load"]] part takes a label-based slice of the downloaded frame: every row from the first downloaded timestamp up to and including LAST_FULL_HOUR (the training cutoff end_train, Section 14.5.6), keeping only the Actual Load column. Label slicing with .loc is inclusive on both ends, so LAST_FULL_HOUR itself is retained; the double brackets return a one-column DataFrame rather than a Series, which is the shape visualize_ts_plotly expects. The trailing .dropna() drops hours ENTSO-E has not yet published, so the plot shows only observed load — the raw, 15-minute “what we downloaded” view (see Section 14.6.3 for the hourly aggregation), before the pipeline’s own outlier removal (Section 14.6.4) and imputation (Section 14.6.5).
The full series spans years of hourly load, so the seasonal shape is visible but the recent days blur together. Figure 14.2 therefore zooms in on the final week — the data closest to the live forecast bridge — with the actuals restricted to the seven days ending at LAST_FULL_HOUR (LAST_WEEK_START = LAST_FULL_HOUR - pd.Timedelta(days=7), then train_view.loc[LAST_WEEK_START:LAST_FULL_HOUR]).
Overlaid on the same axes is ENTSO-E’s own day-ahead Forecasted Load, renamed onto the shared Actual Load column so visualize_ts_plotly draws it as a second trace. In the full-series figure it is clipped to end_train to line up with the actuals; in the last-week figure it is sliced with no right bound (predictions_entsoe.loc[LAST_WEEK_START:]), so its most recent values run past end_train into the published day-ahead forecast for the hours the actuals do not yet cover. It is shown purely for visual context — the forecaster never trains on it (Section 14.6.11).

# requires the plotted column to exist in every frame, so the forecast is
# renamed onto the shared "Actual Load" column; the dict key supplies its

text:
14.6 Lag structure: select key_lags from the data
The autoregressive lags the forecaster considers should follow the data, not a hard-coded guess. Before building the config we read the lag structure straight off the hourly Actual Load and let it pick the lags.
The autocorrelation function (ACF) and partial autocorrelation function (PACF) expose that structure. We select lags with the standard rule: the 95% white-noise significance band is ±1.96/√N, and any correlation outside it is statistically non-zero. We rank candidates by the partial autocorrelation, not the raw ACF — the PACF strips out the correlation already explained by shorter lags, so its significant spikes are the textbook Box–Jenkins signal for which lags carry direct autoregressive information. A raw-ACF threshold (say > 0.8) is unhelpful here: load autocorrelation decays so slowly that nearly every lag would clear it. We keep the strongest few significant lags by |PACF| and feed them into ConfigEntsoe(lags_consider=key_lags) below. They typically recover the hourly persistence (lags 1–3), the daily cycle (around 24), and the weekly cycle (around 168). This works on the raw downloaded series (the hourly mean of the 15-minute actuals, before the pipeline’s own curation), so it diagnoses the genuine lag structure; as Section 14.6.1 explains, the tuned model’s final lags are still chosen by SpotOptim.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from spotforecast2.stats.autocorrelation import calculate_lag_autocorrelation

# Hourly Actual Load over the training side only (mean of each hour's four
# quarter-hour values), matching the grid prepare_data() will build later.
acf_series = interim.loc[:LAST_FULL_HOUR, "Actual Load"].resample("h").mean().dropna()
acf = calculate_lag_autocorrelation(acf_series, n_lags=200)

# Data-driven key lags. The 95% white-noise band is ±1.96/sqrt(N); a lag is
# "significant" when its correlation falls outside it. We rank by the PARTIAL
# autocorrelation (PACF), which removes the correlation already carried by
# shorter lags and so flags only the lags with *direct* predictive value ---
# the standard Box-Jenkins rule. (A raw-ACF threshold is useless here: the load
# ACF decays so slowly that almost every lag clears the band.)
conf = 1.96 / np.sqrt(len(acf_series))
significant = acf[acf["partial_autocorrelation_abs"] > conf]
key_lags = sorted(significant.nlargest(8, "partial_autocorrelation_abs")["lag"].astype(int))
if not key_lags:                       # degenerate fallback (e.g. very short series)
    key_lags = [1, 2, 24, 168]

print(f"N = {len(acf_series)}  |  95% significance band = ±{conf:.4f}")
print(f"significant PACF lags (|pacf| > band): {len(significant)} of {len(acf)}")
print(f"key_lags (top {len(key_lags)} by |PACF|, in lag order): {key_lags}")
print(acf[acf["lag"].isin(key_lags)][
    ["lag", "autocorrelation", "partial_autocorrelation"]

NoteWhere key_lags is used — and who really picks the lags



A natural question is whether lags_consider=key_lags fixes the lags the model forecasts on, or whether the tuner decides. In the tuned spotoptim run this chapter performs (MultiTask(team4_config, task="spotoptim")), the tuner still chooses the winner, but with warm_start_lags=True the data-selected list now genuinely competes. Three steps consume it:

The forecaster factory entsoe_lgbm_factory (spotforecast2/multitask/factories.py) builds the initial forecaster with lags=config.lags_consider[-1] — only the largest entry. With the data-selected key_lags (whose maximum is the weekly lag, around 168), initialize_lags expands that maximum to the full contiguous range 1…max, not the individual selected lags.
SpotOptim treats the lag configuration as a categorical hyperparameter and searches a candidate set. By default that set is hardcoded (_default_spotoptim_search_space in spotforecast2/multitask/search_spaces.py — e.g. "24", "[1, 2, 24, 48]", "[1, 2, 11, 12, 23, 24, 167, 168]"). With warm_start_lags=True, SpotOptimStrategy prepends str(key_lags) to that list, so the PACF-selected lags become a real, selectable candidate.
The same flag seeds the surrogate search: build_warm_start_x0 constructs the optimizer’s first evaluation point at key_lags (combined with the factory’s estimator defaults) and passes it as SpotOptim’s x0, so the seeded configuration is guaranteed to be evaluated rather than left to chance in the random initial design. The winner is applied with set_lags, logged as “Best lags”, and inspectable via exercise 3.

A consequence worth flagging: initialize_lags expands an integer candidate to the contiguous range 1…max, but leaves a list candidate untouched. So when the logged “Best lags” come back gapless (e.g. 1…24), it means the integer candidate "24" won the back-test — not that the search cannot carry gaps. The candidate set above includes genuine non-contiguous sets such as [1, 2, 11, 12, 23, 24, 167, 168], and the winning lags are free to be one of them; the weekly lag survives in the search whether or not it wins.
So under warm_start_lags=True the ACF analysis in 1 no longer only motivates candidate lags — it injects them into the search and seeds the optimizer with them, while the tuner still has the final say among all candidates. With warm_start_lags=False (the default), lags_consider reverts to its passive role: only its maximum (lags_consider[-1]) sizes the pre-tuning forecaster and the minimum history the back-test reserves, and the tuner picks from the hardcoded set alone.

14.6.2 Cross-validation geometry recap
The four constants defined at the top of Section 14.6.1 — PREDICT_SIZE, REFIT_SIZE, NUMBER_FOLDS, and the DELTA_VAL they combine into — do one job: they fix the cross-validation geometry that SpotOptim scores every candidate model against. The config explainer above quoted the result (“the most recent 70 days are held out”); this section derives that number from scratch and shows exactly how the rolling back-test that produces SpotOptim’s objective is laid out. It is self-contained — it reuses the chronological-split idea of Chapter 5 and the rolling-origin back-test of Chapter 10, but every term needed is defined here.

14.6.2.1 Definitions
The pipeline reasons about one contiguous, hourly, gap-free load series. The following terms pin down how that series is carved up for tuning.

Training series

the full hourly Actual Load the tuner is allowed to look at. It runs from start_train to end_train.

end_train

the last timestamp the model may train on — here LAST_FULL_HOUR, the last full hour of published actuals (Section 14.5.6). Everything after it is the live forecast, never part of tuning.

train_size

the length of the training series as a duration. start_train = end_train − train_size. Here three years.

predict_size

the live forecast horizon — how many hours the model is asked to forecast forward in production. The live config sets it to LIVE_N_STEPS (Section 14.5.6), the recursive bridge to tomorrow 23:00, so it is render-dependent (≈ 32). It does not set the cross-validation block; that is cv_block_size.

cv_block_size

the width of each cross-validation test block, in hours — the horizon the folds actually score. The config sets it to PREDICT_SIZE = 24 (one day), fixed and independent of the render-dependent predict_size. Decoupling the two is deliberate: the CV scores a stable 24-hour-ahead block while the live forecast still runs out to LIVE_N_STEPS. (When cv_block_size is left unset it falls back to predict_size — the behaviour chapters 02–11 rely on, where the two coincide at 24.)

delta_val

the validation span: the stretch of the most recent history reserved for evaluation and withheld from the model’s training. It is computed, not chosen directly — see below.

end_cv

the cross-validation training cutoff, end_cv = end_train − delta_val. The model is trained on [start_train, end_cv] and validated on (end_cv, end_train].

Fold

one (train, test) pair. Every fold trains on data ending at or before its test block and predicts the next cv_block_size hours — so a fold never peeks at its own future, the discipline introduced in Chapter 5.

Fold stride

how far the test block advances between consecutive folds. Here it equals cv_block_size = 24, so the folds are back-to-back and non-overlapping: together they tile the whole validation span exactly once.

Rolling-origin back-test

the procedure (Chapter 10) that slides the forecast origin forward one stride at a time across the validation span, collecting a forecast at each step. With refit=False the forecaster is fit once on [start_train, end_cv] and then reused to produce every fold’s forecast — fast, and a deterministic choice (CR-2).

Mean absolute error (MAE)

the score. The fold forecasts are pooled into one vector \(\hat{y}\), compared with the matching actuals \(y\), and averaged: \(\text{MAE} = \tfrac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\lvert y_t - \hat{y}_t\rvert\). This single number, over all validation hours, is what SpotOptim minimises.




14.6.2.2 Computing DELTA_VAL
DELTA_VAL is the product of the other three constants, read as hours:
\[
\texttt{DELTA\_VAL}
  = \underbrace{\texttt{PREDICT\_SIZE}}_{24\ \text{h/fold}}
  \times \underbrace{\texttt{REFIT\_SIZE}}_{7}
  \times \underbrace{\texttt{NUMBER\_FOLDS}}_{10}
  = 24 \times 7 \times 10 = 1680\ \text{h} = 70\ \text{days}.
\]
This span is then sliced off the tail of the training series. With end_cv = end_train − delta_val, the series splits cleanly into a training part and a validation part whose lengths add up to train_size:
\[
\underbrace{\texttt{train\_size}}_{3\ \text{yr}\,=\,26280\ \text{h}}
  = \underbrace{(\texttt{train\_size} - \texttt{delta\_val})}_{\text{CV training window}}
  + \underbrace{\texttt{delta\_val}}_{\text{validation span}}
  = 24600\ \text{h} + 1680\ \text{h}.
\]
The fold count then falls straight out of the geometry. The folds are non-overlapping blocks of cv_block_size = 24 hours that tile the validation span, so their number is
\[
\#\text{folds}
  = \frac{\texttt{delta\_val}}{\texttt{cv\_block\_size}}
  = \frac{1680}{24}
  = \texttt{REFIT\_SIZE} \times \texttt{NUMBER\_FOLDS}
  = 7 \times 10 = 70,
\]
and the total validation hours scored is \(70 \times 24 = 1680 =
\texttt{delta\_val}\). The 70/70 progress bars at Section 14.6.8 are exactly this count, the same for every render. The clean identity holds because we set cv_block_size = PREDICT_SIZE. Had the CV instead inherited the live predict_size = LIVE_N_STEPS (≈ 32 h) — as it did before the cv_block_size field existed — the block would tile the span into ⌈1680 / 32⌉ = 53 folds, and the count would drift render to render with the feed’s freshness (Section 14.5.6). Decoupling the CV block from the live horizon is exactly what cv_block_size buys.
A note on the names, so the arithmetic is not mistaken for behaviour the code does not have. In this cross-validation the model is fit once and reused (refit=False), so REFIT_SIZE does not trigger any refitting — it is one of two factors whose product, with PREDICT_SIZE, sizes the held-out span. Likewise NUMBER_FOLDS enters only through that product; because we set cv_block_size = PREDICT_SIZE, the real fold count is the 70 derived above, not 10. The constants are a convenient way to spell a 70-day window as “ten weekly blocks of daily forecasts”, not a description of a ten-fold refit loop. (Internally cv_ts in spotforecast2 reads cv_block_size — falling back to predict_size when it is unset — sets end_cv = end_train − delta_val, and returns a TimeSeriesFold(steps=cv_block_size, refit=False, allow_incomplete_fold=True) — the same TimeSeriesFold machinery used in Chapter 10.)
