folds: 1680 / cv_block_size = 1680 / 24 = 70 non-overlapping daily blocks tiling the 70-day span — the same count for every render, because cv_block_size is fixed at 24 and does not track the live predict_size;
scored hours: 70 × 24 = 1680 = delta_val, pooled into the single MAE SpotOptim drives down.



14.6.2.5 How SpotOptim consumes it
This geometry is the fixed yardstick of the search. Each SpotOptim trial proposes one hyperparameter candidate — including a lag set, the warm-started key_lags among them (Section 14.6.1) — builds the forecaster, runs the 70-fold rolling back-test above, and returns its pooled MAE. The surrogate optimiser then picks the next candidate to try, always against the same 1680-hour validation window tiled the same way every render, so trials are directly comparable. Exercise 3 inspects which lag configuration ultimately won.






NoteWhy cv_block_size is a separate knob



The config carries two horizons that are easy to confuse. predict_size = LIVE_N_STEPS is the live forecast horizon — the recursive bridge to tomorrow 23:00, which floats with the ENTSO-E feed’s freshness at render time (≈ 25–48 h). cv_block_size = 24 is the cross-validation block — the horizon each fold scores. Setting them apart matters for two reasons:

The search minimises the pooled MAE of cv_block_size-step-ahead forecasts. Fixing that at a 24-hour day keeps the tuning objective aligned with the leaderboard’s 24-hour metric, instead of a longer, render-dependent horizon.
Because cv_block_size is constant, the validation protocol (block width and the 1680/24 = 70 fold count) is identical across renders — the reproducibility (CR-2) the frozen chapters enjoy, now kept for the live one.

Were the two coupled — cv_block_size left unset, so the CV inherited predict_size = LIVE_N_STEPS — the block would be ≈ 32 h, the fold count ⌈1680/32⌉ = 53, and both would drift between renders. That coupling is exactly what the cv_block_size field (added in spotforecast2-safe) removes; Exercise 4 probes how much the choice of block actually moves the tuned model.

14.6.4 Step 2 — Outlier detection and curation
Curation needs a bound. A fixed pair such as ±1e9 MW flags nothing, so it removes nothing; a tight pair risks deleting genuine demand — the January cold-snap peaks and the holiday troughs are real records the model must see. We want the opposite of both: bounds wide enough to keep every plausible value, narrow enough to excise the physically impossible ones (a reported 0 MW national load, a sensor spike to ten times the peak).
We therefore derive the bounds from the load history itself, using a robust rule that the anomalies cannot distort. Let \(m\) be the median of the series and \(\mathrm{IQR}\) its inter-quartile range (the 75th minus the 25th percentile). Median and IQR are robust: a handful of absurd records barely moves them, so the band they define is not inflated by the very points we mean to catch. The bounds are
\[
\text{lower} = \max(0,\; m - K\cdot\mathrm{IQR}), \qquad
\text{upper} = m + K\cdot\mathrm{IQR},
\]
with \(K = 5\) — a deliberately relaxed width. (For reference, Tukey’s “far out” fence uses \(K = 3\); ours is wider still.) For German load this places the band at roughly \([0,\,130]\) GW, so only records outside any plausible national demand are flagged. The lower bound is floored at 0 MW because load cannot be negative. OUTLIER_IQR_K is exposed as a constant: lower it to curate more aggressively, raise it to curate only the most extreme records.
We compute the bounds from the prepared history and assign them to team4_mt.config.bounds before detection runs.

detect_outliers() snapshots the pre-curation series into df_pipeline_original, then replaces every value outside these bounds with NaN in df_pipeline via manual_outlier_removal (the values are replaced, not clipped to the bound). The second branch of detect_outliers() runs an IsolationForest pass (get_outliers, contamination=0.01), but that call only reports candidate anomalies to the log — it does not alter the series. The hard bounds are therefore the sole mechanism that marks NaN. Removing implausible values here is a direct Art. 10 data governance obligation: the model must not learn from corrupted records.
What happens to a flagged record next is the substance of curation, and it is not deletion. The recursive LightGBM forecaster reads autoregressive lags off a contiguous hourly index; dropping rows outright would misalign every downstream lag. Instead, Step 3 (Section 14.6.5) imputes the NaN with the default weighted strategy: it forward/back-fills the gap so the index stays gap-free, and it builds a sample-weight function that assigns weight 0 to each imputed timestamp and the surrounding imputation_window_size h (here 24 h). That weight function is threaded into the forecaster (ForecasterRecursive(weight_func=…)), so during fit the curated rows contribute nothing to the training loss and nothing to the validation score. A flagged record is thus replaced by NaN, filled only to preserve lag continuity, and excluded from training and validation by zero weight — the intended Art. 10 outcome, reached without breaking the recursive feature construction.
imputation_window_size is a dedicated knob: it sets the gap-penalty width independently of window_size (default 72 h), which still controls the LightGBM rolling-mean feature window. During tuning SpotOptim evaluates many short cross-validation folds, and a fold lying entirely inside a penalty zone has every row at weight 0; the forecaster then logs “all sample weights for the requested index are zero … using uniform weighting” and falls back to uniform weights for that fold. This is benign — it is the safe degenerate case, not an error — but a narrower imputation_window_size makes it rarer without widening the rolling-feature window.

14.6.7 Processing of the Weather Data
build_exogenous_features() pulls weather from the Open-Meteo API through get_weather_features() (in spotforecast2_safe.weather.features). It fetches hourly temperature_2m — the dominant load driver below ~5 °C and above ~15 °C — plus fourteen other variables for the Dortmund default location (51.5136 °N, 7.4653 °E; the state="NW" setting drives the holiday calendar, not the weather coordinates), caches them as a parquet file, and derives the rolling 1-day and 7-day mean/max/min window features enabled by include_weather_windows=True. The result is stored as team4_mt.weather_aligned and plotted against load below.
The interesting part is the recent edge of the series, because Open-Meteo serves two endpoints with a coverage seam. The archive endpoint carries quality-checked history but lags about five days; the forecast endpoint carries today and the days ahead, and — via its past_days parameter — a configurable number of recent days backwards. _fetch_hybrid() stitches them together: it takes the archive up to now - 5 days and the forecast with enough past_days to bridge that five-day lag plus enough forecast_days to reach the prediction horizon. This is the weather analogue of the ENTSO-E publication lag in Section 14.5.7: the most recent days are not yet in the historical record.
A worked example makes the seam concrete. The cell below recomputes, for this render, the two numbers that close it.

That seam is exactly where missing weather data must be handled correctly. After fetching, the frame is reindexed onto a regular hourly grid spanning [data_start, cov_end], where cov_end is end_train plus the predict_size horizon. Two fail-loud tiers then govern any remaining gap, both active because the safe default fill_missing=False applies:

The fetch layer (_finalize_df) rejects any interior NaN or absent hour and reports the offending timestamps, rather than filling them. Example: a single missing hour 2026-05-20 03:00 raises with that timestamp listed.
The alignment layer (get_weather_features) forward-fills only short gaps, up to MAX_FFILL_GAP_PERIODS = 24 consecutive hours; a longer run raises WeatherFetchError. Last observation carried forward (LOCF) is acceptable for a brief outage but not for days. Example: a 3-hour gap holds the 02:00 reading (say 8.4 °C) across 03:00–05:00 — a run of 3 ≤ 24, tolerated. A 120-hour gap (2026-05-26…2026-05-30) is a run of 120 > 24, so it raises WeatherFetchError, which on_weather_failure="skip" catches: the model then trains without weather for that run instead of on a five-day flat line.

This refusal is a direct Art. 10 obligation: a carried-forward value must not masquerade as a measurement, and a multi-day flat temperature would corrupt the single most important exogenous driver. The same data-governance stance appears in Section 14.6.4 and Section 14.6.5.
Because the recent window is now genuinely fetched, Figure 14.9 shows real diurnal temperature variation across the last week of training data — cold spells lifting the load — rather than a flat tail.

14.6.8 Step 5 — Train with SpotOptim and predict through tomorrow
With the curated, gap-free target and the selected exogenous matrix in place, run() executes the SpotOptim search and refits the LGBM forecaster. With the advanced configuration this cell typically takes 5–10 minutes on a recent laptop — mostly the SpotOptim trials against the CV folds.






NoteReading the SpotOptim progress bars



Because the cell below calls run(show=True), SpotOptim prints a tqdm progress bar every time it scores a candidate model — one bar per rolling cross-validation back-test. The numbers to the right of a finished bar, e.g. 70/70 [00:00<00:00, 259.84it/s], are tqdm’s standard read-out:

70/70 — steps completed out of the total; here all 70 are done (100 %).
[00:00<00:00, 259.84it/s] follows the pattern [elapsed<remaining, rate]:

the first 00:00 is the wall-clock time already spent on the bar (mm:ss, or h:mm:ss once it passes an hour);
the second 00:00 is tqdm’s estimate of the time still to go — zero here, because the bar has just finished;
259.84it/s is the throughput, about 260 iterations per second; below one per second tqdm switches to its reciprocal s/it (seconds per iteration).


A bar caught mid-run, 55/70 [00:00<00:00, 240.00it/s], would then read: 55 of 70 steps done, at about 240 steps per second.
The total, 70, is the number of folds in the back-test that scores one candidate. The search reserves a validation span of delta_val = PREDICT_SIZE × REFIT_SIZE × NUMBER_FOLDS = 24 × 7 × 10 = 1680 hours (70 days, Section 14.6.2) and tiles it into blocks of cv_block_size hours. The config sets cv_block_size = PREDICT_SIZE = 24, decoupled from the live predict_size = LIVE_N_STEPS (Section 14.5.6), so
\[
\#\text{folds} = \frac{\texttt{delta\_val}}{\texttt{cv\_block\_size}}
              = \frac{1680}{24} = 70 .
\]
Because cv_block_size is fixed, this total is the same on every render — it does not drift with the live horizon. One such bar appears for roughly every candidate the search scores (n_initial_spotoptim + n_trials_spotoptim). Section 14.6.2 derives this geometry in full and explains why the CV block is cv_block_size, not the live predict_size.
These bars are progress reporting only. They do not affect the result. Passing show=False (as Chapter 13 does) suppresses them entirely.

The day-ahead forecast reaches the interim file because the download in Section 14.5.2 passes keep_forecast_future=True (without it, download_new_data drops every future row). title: 15  ENTSO-E day-ahead baseline submission
text:
15.1 Overview
Chapter 13 tunes an Optuna LightGBM forecaster; Chapter 14 tunes a richer SpotOptim variant. Both pull ENTSO-E’s own day-ahead Forecasted Load purely as a comparison overlay (Section 14.6.11) and never let the model train on it. This chapter inverts that relationship: it submits ENTSO-E’s day-ahead forecast directly, with no model at all.
That is deliberate. ENTSO-E aggregates the forecasts the European transmission system operators already produce for grid scheduling, so it is a strong, free, professionally-maintained baseline. A tuned model that cannot beat it over the rolling 7-day window is not earning its compute. Submitting it as its own team entsoe puts that yardstick on the public leaderboard next to the student models, where the comparison is unavoidable.
Every safety contract from Chapter 13 carries over unchanged (24-row schema, strictly-positive forecasts, no NaN). What disappears is the entire modelling stack: no MultiTask, no ConfigEntsoe, no tuning, no exogenous features. The forecast is a slice of the downloaded ENTSO-E frame. Two wrinkles specific to a forward baseline are handled along the way — the safe downloader drops future rows unless asked to keep them (Section 15.5.2), and a UTC target day straddles two local publication days (Section 15.5.3).

15.5 Live pipeline

import os
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

# Isolate this chapter's storage from chapters 13 and 14 (each pins its own
# download home so the three chapters never read or write the same interim
# file). The package reads the env var at call time via get_data_home().
os.environ["SPOTFORECAST2_DATA"]  = str(Path.home() / "spotforecast2_data"  / "ddmo_ch15_entsoe")
os.environ["SPOTFORECAST2_CACHE"] = str(Path.home() / ".spotforecast2_cache" / "ddmo_ch15_entsoe")

from spotforecast2_safe.downloader.entsoe import download_new_data
from spotforecast2_safe.data.fetch_data import get_data_home

api_key = os.environ.get("ENTSOE_API_KEY")
assert api_key, "ENTSOE_API_KEY must be set in the environment (see @sec-live-walkthrough Step 3)."


15.5.1 Dynamic date constants
Every date is derived from pd.Timestamp.now(tz="UTC").normalize() so the chapter stays correct on every render — same convention as Section 13.5. y_0 is tomorrow’s UTC day (00:00–23:00 UTC), the 24 hourly stamps the leaderboard scores.

NOW_UTC = pd.Timestamp.now(tz="UTC")
TODAY_UTC = NOW_UTC.normalize()
TOMORROW_UTC = TODAY_UTC + pd.Timedelta(days=1)
LAST_TARGET = TOMORROW_UTC + pd.Timedelta(hours=23)

# A day-ahead baseline needs no training history --- only a short recent window:
# enough to carry the last week of `Actual Load` for the context plot plus a
# previous-day fallback (@sec-entsoe-extract). We download the last 10 days and
# reach the end through the day *after* tomorrow so the full target day is
# covered as soon as ENTSO-E publishes it. download_new_data takes the window as
# 'YYYYMMDDHH00' strings.
START_DOWNLOAD = (TODAY_UTC - pd.Timedelta(days=10)).strftime("%Y%m%d%H%M")
END_DOWNLOAD = (TOMORROW_UTC + pd.Timedelta(days=1)).strftime("%Y%m%d%H%M")

print(f"NOW_UTC        = {NOW_UTC}")
print(f"TODAY_UTC      = {TODAY_UTC}")
print(f"TOMORROW_UTC   = {TOMORROW_UTC}  (target day = y_0)")
print(f"LAST_TARGET    = {LAST_TARGET}")
print(f"START_DOWNLOAD = {START_DOWNLOAD}  (10 days back --- no training history)")
print(f"END_DOWNLOAD   = {END_DOWNLOAD}  (covers tomorrow's day-ahead forecast)")

LAST_TARGET    = 2026-06-01 23:00:00+00:00
START_DOWNLOAD = 202605210000  (10 days back --- no training history)
END_DOWNLOAD   = 202606020000  (covers tomorrow's day-ahead forecast)




15.5.2 Download ENTSO-E’s day-ahead Forecasted Load
We fetch through the same safe wrapper the training chapters use, spotforecast2_safe.downloader.entsoe.download_new_data, with one argument that matters here: keep_forecast_future=True. By default the wrapper drops every row after now when it merges the download into the interim file —
# spotforecast2_safe/downloader/entsoe.py
if not keep_forecast_future:
    merged_df = merged_df.loc[merged_df.index <= pd.Timestamp.now(tz="UTC")]
That truncation is correct for the training chapters (a model must never see the future), but it would erase the very thing this baseline submits: ENTSO-E’s day-ahead Forecasted Load for tomorrow. The flag keeps those future rows; future Actual Load is still blank, so nothing leaks — there is no model here in any case. ENTSO-E’s Forecasted Load is published per local (Europe/Berlin) day; the wrapper normalises the merged interim index to UTC, the zone the leaderboard scores in.

download_new_data(
    api_key=api_key,
    country_code="DE",
    start=START_DOWNLOAD,
    end=END_DOWNLOAD,
    force=True,
    keep_forecast_future=True,   # keep tomorrow's day-ahead forecast
)

interim_csv = get_data_home() / "interim" / "energy_load.csv"
interim = pd.read_csv(interim_csv, index_col=0, parse_dates=True)
interim.index = pd.to_datetime(interim.index, utc=True)

print(f"columns            : {list(interim.columns)}")
print(f"Forecasted Load to : {interim['Forecasted Load'].dropna().index.max()}")
print(f"Actual Load to     : {interim['Actual Load'].dropna().index.max()}")

15.5.3 Assemble the 24-hour target slice
The target is the 24 UTC hours of tomorrow, 00:00 … 23:00. ENTSO-E publishes its day-ahead forecast per local (Europe/Berlin) day, and Germany runs one or two hours ahead of UTC. So at submission time — the afternoon of D-1, when only the local D day-ahead is out — the last one or two UTC hours of the target (22:00, 23:00 UTC) fall into the next local day, which ENTSO-E does not publish until D, after the D-1 23:59 UTC deadline.
Those trailing hours are therefore filled with ENTSO-E’s own forecast for the same clock hour 24 hours earlier — a transparent, fully reproducible persistence of the operators’ published forecast (today’s day-ahead is already complete, so the fallback source always exists). The fill is logged, and a fail-loud guard (CR-3) aborts if even the fallback is missing rather than writing a short or NaN-padded CSV.

target_index = pd.date_range(TOMORROW_UTC, LAST_TARGET, freq="h", tz="UTC")  # 24 stamps
y0 = forecast_h.reindex(target_index)

published = int(y0.notna().sum())
missing = y0.index[y0.isna()]
print(f"day-ahead hours published for {TOMORROW_UTC.date()}: {published} / 24")

for ts in missing:
    fallback = forecast_h.reindex([ts - pd.Timedelta(days=1)]).iloc[0]
    if pd.isna(fallback):
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"No day-ahead value for {ts} and no 24 h-earlier fallback either; "
            "ENTSO-E coverage is too thin to assemble 24 hours. Re-render once "
            "the day-ahead forecast for the target day is published."
        )
    y0.loc[ts] = fallback
    print(f"  filled {ts} ← {ts - pd.Timedelta(days=1)} (24 h-earlier ENTSO-E forecast = {fallback:,.0f} MW)")

y0.name = "Forecasted Load"
print(f"\ny_0 assembled: {len(y0)} hourly steps | {y0.index.min()} → {y0.index.max()}")
print(y0)

text:
15.7 Why a baseline team
The leaderboard ranks on rolling 7-day mean MAE (Section 13.2). Without a reference point, a student team has no way to tell whether an MAE of, say, 1500 MW is good. The entsoe row supplies that reference: it is the accuracy the operators’ own forecast achieves on the very same scoring rule. Three readings follow directly from its position on the board:

A team above entsoe is beating the professional day-ahead forecast — a genuine result worth writing up.
A team below entsoe is being out-predicted by a free public series and should revisit features or tuning before adding compute.
entsoe’s own day-to-day MAE variance shows the irreducible difficulty of each target day — a calm Sunday scores tighter than a volatile cold snap, for everyone.







TipExercises (with Claude)




Score the baseline yourself. Once tomorrow becomes a past day with published actuals, re-query query_load_and_forecast, align forecast_h with the realised Actual Load, and compute the 24-hour MAE by hand. Compare it to the leaderboard’s scored value.
Beat it on one day. Render Chapter 14 for the same target day and compare its y_0 against this baseline’s y_0. On which hours does the tuned model diverge most from ENTSO-E, and does that help or hurt once the actuals land?
Probe the boundary fill. How many UTC hours did the fallback in Section 15.5.3 supply today, and why does that count change with the season (CET vs CEST)? Discuss with Claude whether a smarter fill than 24 h persistence (e.g. the same weekday last week) would be worth the complexity for one or two hours.
